newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - Egypt's new investor incentive law raises eyebrows.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Egypt's new investor incentive law raises eyebrows.

text.p: Egypt has scrapped a remnant of central planning with a new law to infuse the economy with fresh investment, but some investors are lobbying the government to ensure firms already in Egypt retain their incentives.

Such issues are crucial as the country tries to draw local and foreign funds in the hope of becoming a regional "tiger" economy like those in Asia. Egypt has privatised earnestly since President Hosni Mubarak set up a reform-minded cabinet in 1996.
Ibrahim Fawzy, president of Egypt's General Authority for Investment (GAFI), said the new incentives law, which took effect in May, cuts red tape to make it easier to set up firms.
Investors simply notify GAFI that their project is among 15 priority fields, including land reclamation and infrastructure.
"This is our new philosophy," Fawzy said. "Establishing the company takes one day. I do it all here. In the old days I used to get permission from the prime minister.

"In the old days we used to approve projects individually in line with the centrally planned economy. Our economy has now reached a reasonable plateau. We approve fields. The philosophy here is we want to affect development," he said.
LAW REFLECTS DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES

The law reflects Egypt's priorities to attract funds to less developed areas with a scale of incentives. It gives a 20-year tax break for investors in Toskha and the New Valley, Mubarak's pet project. Satellite cities, remote areas and new industrial zones get a 10-year break and city investors get five years.
Another feature is that the government can give away land to investors who set up projects in priority fields including manufacturing, hotels, cargo and silos, housing and brokerages.
Egypt hopes investment will grow.
GAFI says $3.9 billion in investment proposals were approved in the first quarter of 1997 compared to $681 million in the same period in 1996.
Minister of State for Economic Affairs Youssef Boutros-Ghali told Reuters foreign direct investment was expected to grow to $1.5 billion in 1997 from $800 million to $900 million in 1996.
But when Egypt showcased the law at a conference in May, reactions were mixed. Some say it is unclear how projects already set up will benefit.
"It is a very bad law," Peter Smit of Proctor and Gamble in Egypt told the conference. He told Reuters his concern focused on how, if at all, tax benefits of previous laws would be retained.
LOBBYING FOR CHANGES
American and German chambers of commerce are lobbying to influence the law's statutes to be issued in three months, and some of their concerns also involve tax benefits.

"There have been a couple of issues not addressed in the law and which we hope soon will be covered in the executive regulations. The previous law used to extend tax incentives for any capital increase or any extension of the project. This is not covered," said Ahmed Shawki, American chamber president.

He said the new law also does not spell out incentives for small businesses and newly privatised firms. "We had some points which we sent to the prime minister. Maybe the executive regulations can spell out all these things," Shawki said.
May Durra of the German-Arab Chamber of Commerce said the group decided on June 1 to send a memo to the government asking for changes in the law as it affects existing companies.

"They omitted the article concerning the expansion of the existing companies," she said. "It says that under the old law you have a tax holiday when you expand your company. They omitted (it) and focused on whatever projects and activities... or companies that are going to be in the New Valley. They didn't say anything about the existing companies in the old valley."
Durra said her members sought more say on joint-venture boards and to ease import regulations for multinationals.
"They think these things are more important than just giving them tax holidays for 10 or 20 years," Durra said.
